transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… what finally made me come in is this thing that happens when I’m driving toward Miami and I get to one of those long bridges. It’s almost immediate, like my car reaches the bridge and my whole body reacts before I can talk myself out of it. My chest tightens, my hands just clamp down on the steering wheel, and I get this sudden, very strong feeling that I have to get off the bridge right then.

And of course there’s nowhere to go, which makes it feel worse. I know that sounds… I don’t know, maybe unreasonable, but in the moment it feels absolutely certain, like I can’t just keep going. That’s really what pushed me to come talk to someone.
Does this reaction happen only when you’re on long bridges?

Yes, it’s really those long bridges toward Miami that set it off in that immediate way. It’s not something I sit there building up to for miles, exactly — it’s like the second my car actually reaches the bridge, my body just reacts. My chest tightens, my hands grip the steering wheel so hard, and I get this awful, sudden feeling that I have to get off the bridge right away.

And the worst part is knowing there’s nowhere to pull off or turn around, so it makes that feeling even sharper. I know, sitting here, that it probably sounds out of proportion, but when I’m actually on the bridge, it feels absolutely certain in my mind that I need to get off.
Have you ever had one of these sudden episodes when you were not on a long bridge?

No… not in that same sudden way. I mean, I can think about the drive beforehand and feel uneasy, but that real episode—the chest tightening, my hands locking onto the wheel, that instant certainty that I have to get off right now—that happens when the car actually reaches one of those long bridges toward Miami.

It’s very tied to that moment, because once I’m on it, there’s nowhere to go, and that’s when my body seems to react before I’ve even had a chance to reason with myself.
When you’re on the bridge, is the scariest part that you can’t easily get off or escape?

Yes… yes, I think that’s a big part of it. It’s that feeling of being trapped on it, I suppose. The moment my car actually reaches one of those long bridges toward Miami, it’s like my body realizes before my mind does that there’s no easy way off. My chest tightens, my hands just clamp down on the steering wheel, and I get this sudden certainty—almost like an alarm going off—that I have to get off the bridge right then.

And of course I know, logically, that I can’t just do that. There’s nowhere to pull over or turn around, and that seems to make it worse. It’s not just disliking the bridge—it’s that once I’m on it, I feel stuck there until it ends, and my whole body reacts as if I need to escape immediately.
Do you get the same trapped, urgent need-to-escape feeling in other situations where you can’t easily get out?

Not really in the same way, no. I mean, I can feel uncomfortable in other places where I know I can’t just leave easily, but what finally made me come in is very specific: the moment my car reaches one of those long bridges toward Miami, my chest tightens, my hands clamp down on the wheel, and I get this sudden certainty that I have to get off.

It’s almost embarrassing to say because I know there isn’t anywhere to go, and that’s part of what makes it so awful. But that urgent “I have to escape right now” feeling—that really happens on those bridges.
When you’re on the bridge, are you mainly afraid that you’ll have a sudden panic attack there?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. I mean, I don’t think I’m sitting there thinking, “What if I have a panic attack?” exactly. It’s more… I notice the feeling once it’s already happening, if that makes sense.

When I get onto the bridge, I’m mostly aware of being stuck there and needing it to be over, needing to get off. I suppose the physical feeling is frightening too, of course, but I don’t know that the fear is about having an attack so much as being on that bridge and not being able to do anything about it. It all kind of comes together in the moment.
Do you avoid long bridges because of this fear?

Yes, I do. More than I like to admit, actually. I’ve started saying no to things I would have gone to without a second thought before—gallery openings, little birdwatching outings, even visits with my daughter—if I know it means I’d have to drive over one of those long bridges myself.

Sometimes I try to arrange it so someone else drives me, and if that’s possible then I can usually make myself go. But if I’m the one who has to be behind the wheel over the bridge, I’ll find some reason not to go, or I’ll put it off, or I’ll say I’m tired. It embarrasses me terribly, because I’ve always been the one who planned things, handled the driving, got myself where I needed to be. I don’t like feeling dependent on someone else just because of a bridge, but that’s what’s been happening.
Aside from long bridges, do you also avoid tunnels?

Tunnels… I’m not really sure. I don’t think I avoid them in the same way, no. I mean, I can’t immediately think of changing plans because of a tunnel the way I have with the long bridges.

I suppose if I were in a very long tunnel I might not love it, but it’s not something I’ve noticed myself planning around or dreading ahead of time. The bridge thing is the one that’s been standing out to me.
When you’re on those bridges, are you afraid of the height?

I don’t think it’s the height exactly. At least, that’s not what I’m aware of.

I’m not looking over the side thinking, “Oh, it’s so high up,” or imagining falling, really. I usually keep my eyes on the road, and it’s more the whole situation of being on the bridge that gets to me. But the height itself… no, I can’t say that’s the main thing. If anything, I almost don’t want to look around enough to know how high it is.
When you’re on those long bridges, are you mainly afraid of being over the water?

Yes… I think that’s closer to it. It’s the water, or maybe the feeling of being out over all that open space with water underneath, with nowhere to pull over or get off quickly. I know that sounds a little irrational even as I say it.

I mean, I know perfectly well those bridges have been there for years. People drive across them all day long, every day, and nothing happens. I can tell myself that. I do tell myself that. But when it’s me, and I’m thinking about driving over all that open water, the fear just becomes much bigger than the actual danger. It’s as if my mind knows one thing, but my body reacts as though it’s something terribly risky.
